Barcode Magic

ArithmeticDivisibilityNumber Theory
Game: A product code has twelve digits. Leave one out and the computer can tell you which digit is missing.
How to play: Click the right half of a digit to make it bigger, or the left half to make it smaller, until eleven digits are set. Press Check to hear what the computer says.

Click the right half of a number to count up, or the left half to count down. You can also use the arrow keys while a number is chosen.

Look for the math

The last digit on a product's label is not chosen by the maker at random. It is a checksum: it is picked so that a sum of the twelve digits comes out even. That one condition is enough to rebuild any single digit you hide.

The twelve-digit rule

A UPC-A code has twelve digits. Give the digits in the odd places (the 1st, 3rd, … 11th) a weight of 3, and the ones in the even places a weight of 1. Their total must be a multiple of ten:

3·d1 + d2 + 3·d3 + d4 + … + 3·d11 + d12 ≡ 0 (mod 10)

The applet starts with twelve question marks and a click steps any one of them through 0, 1, …, 9 and back to a question mark, so you can type in any code you like.

Why the answer is forced

Working modulo 10, both weights 1 and 3 can be undone: 1 undoes itself and 3 is undone by 7 (because 3 × 7 = 21, which leaves 1). If the blank is in an even place the computer works out 7 × (10 − sum mod 10) mod 10; in an odd place it just uses (10 − sum mod 10) mod 10. Either way there is exactly one digit that can go in the gap. That is the whole trick.

What the picture shows

Under the digits is the code drawn as a barcode. Each digit becomes seven narrow modules: the first six digits use one pattern (odd parity) and the last six use its opposite (even parity), with 101 at each end and 01010 in the middle. A question mark is drawn as one solid block.

Did the page's claims check out?

The logic test tried all 12,000 ways to hide one digit in a valid code made from any first three digits: the computer got the hidden digit right every time. It also checked that a new code shows twelve question marks, that clicking reaches every decimal digit, and that the bars match the applet's own pattern tables. One quirk was kept: the original runs the answer straight after the word "is" with no space, so the message reads "The missing digit is7".

Try hiding the first digit and then the last. The multiplier changes from 7 to 1, but the answer is still forced.
